notes.summary: A–B: actual balanced full-test minimizers give V=nW/H and the same cost for every attaining selection. Fixed-test limits identify the nef endpoint and prove the finite improper identity for every smooth a, without an endpoint PDE or regularity of metric selections.
notes.detailedSummary: The permitted closed base Monge–Ampère theorem supplies A_epsilon^m=(W/H)sigma/(a+epsilon). The metric gamma=(a+epsilon)^(-1/m)(A_epsilon+(a+epsilon)w) is balanced. Matrix AM–GM proves the lower bound for every Gauduchon test, and gamma attains equality. Differentiability of the explicit value and a supporting-line argument determine every minimizer's cost, including s=0 by strict extension. Fixed-test comparison identifies the raw endpoint infimum with both the path limit and decreasing Hermitian regularization. Monotone convergence gives V_endpoint=nW/H(0), interpreted as zero for an infinite inverse moment. Ordinary calculus then proves the finite improper integral for every minimizing selection. Only the expressly permitted smooth positive closed-class existence theorem is imported.
notes.text:
This note proves restricted targets A and B for the exact product probability in the assignment. Write n=m+1, a in C-infinity(B), L=a+epsilon with epsilon=t-s>0, H(epsilon)=integral_B L^(-1) sigma, J(epsilon)=integral_B L^(-2) sigma, and W=integral_B alpha^m. Pullbacks to X=B x C are implicit. A smooth area form w on the curve is d-closed for dimensional reasons. Hence Omega=alpha+w is a Kähler metric on X and is itself a Gauduchon test; the test set is nonempty. Theta_s=alpha+Lw is positive. Theta_t=alpha+aw is semipositive, so theta_t+delta h>0 for every delta>0 with zero potential. Thus the endpoint is nef in the specified Hermitian definition.

The only imported PDE is the expressly permitted smooth positive-data theorem in a strict closed Kähler class. Its indispensable statement was checked against Tosatti–Weinkove, https://arxiv.org/pdf/0910.1390v2, Corollary 1 on printed page 1 and the closed normalization on printed page 2. Their potential convention is i partial barpartial; multiplying the source potential by 2 pi gives the present dd^c. The density constant is zero for a closed background when the total masses coincide, by smooth Stokes. Here rho_epsilon=(W/H) sigma/L is smooth positive and has total mass W. The theorem therefore supplies a genuine global smooth phi_epsilon with
  A_epsilon=alpha+dd^c phi_epsilon>0, d A_epsilon=0,
  A_epsilon^m=(W/H) sigma/L.
Closedness also gives integral_B A_epsilon^m=W directly: expand the power and integrate each term containing dd^c phi_epsilon by Stokes against its remaining closed factors. Existence is used independently at each epsilon; continuity or differentiability of epsilon -> phi_epsilon is not presumed.

Put Psi=A_epsilon+Lw and v=nW/H. Since w^2=0 and horizontal forms above degree 2m vanish,
  Psi^n=n L A_epsilon^m wedge w=v mu,
  gamma=L^(-1/m) Psi,
  gamma^m=A_epsilon^m/L+m A_epsilon^(m-1) wedge w.
Gamma is a smooth positive Hermitian metric. The first term of gamma^m is a horizontal top-degree form, so its exterior derivative vanishes even for nonconstant L. The second is closed because A_epsilon and w are closed. Thus d gamma^m=0 and dd^c gamma^m=0: gamma is an actual balanced Gauduchon test.

For ANY smooth positive Gauduchon metric xi on X, Stokes and dd^c xi^m=0 imply
  integral_X theta_s wedge xi^m=integral_X Psi wedge xi^m.
No product structure or closedness of xi is assumed. Diagonalize Psi relative to xi at a point, with positive eigenvalues r_1,...,r_n. The wedge identities and matrix AM–GM give
  (Psi wedge xi^m)/xi^n=(r_1+...+r_n)/n
    >=(r_1...r_n)^(1/n)=(Psi^n/xi^n)^(1/n).
Using Psi^n=v mu and integrating yields
  integral_X theta_s wedge xi^m>=v^(1/n) D_mu(xi).
The denominator is positive and finite on the compact manifold. This lower bound holds for every participating test, including arbitrary nonproduct Gauduchon metrics.

For the constructed metric,
  gamma^n=v L^(-n/m) mu,
  D_mu(gamma)=v^(m/n) integral_X L^(-1) mu=v^(m/n) H,
  integral_X theta_s wedge gamma^m=integral_X Psi wedge gamma^m=v H.
The probability normalization integral_C w=1 is used exactly. Gamma therefore attains the full infimum, and
  lambda_mu(theta_s)=(nW/H)^(1/n),
  V_mu(theta_s)=nW/H.
This is full-test equality and actual minimizing-test existence. The answer retains the specified probability sigma wedge w: the shape of w cancels through its mass-one normalization, whereas the inverse moment H retains sigma.

For gamma the cost numerator is
  integral_X w wedge gamma^m=integral_B A_epsilon^m/L=(W/H)J.
After division by D_mu(gamma), its cost is
  C(s)=n^(-m/n) W^(1/n) H^(-(n+1)/n) J.
To prove the same cost for every attaining metric, define
  Q_r(xi)=integral_X theta_r wedge xi^m/D_mu(xi),
  c_xi=integral_X w wedge xi^m/D_mu(xi).
If xi attains at s, then at each neighboring strict point r,
  lambda_mu(theta_r)<=Q_r(xi)
    =lambda_mu(theta_s)-(r-s)c_xi.
On compact strict intervals L has a uniform positive lower bound, so dominated differentiation gives dH/ds=J. Differentiating the explicit value gives
  d/ds lambda_mu(theta_s)
    =-n^(-m/n) W^(1/n) H^(-(n+1)/n)J.
Divide the supporting-line inequality by r-s first for r>s and then for r<s. Taking limits forces -c_xi to equal this derivative. Thus every attaining xi has cost C(s). The argument includes s=0 because the same strictly positive path and formulas extend to all real s<t, including negative s. No metric uniqueness or differentiable metric family is used.

Define the raw endpoint infimum over the same full test set by
  E=inf_xi integral_X theta_t wedge xi^m/D_mu(xi).
It is nonnegative by semipositivity and finite by testing Omega. For each fixed xi,
  Q_(t-epsilon)(xi)=Q_t(xi)+epsilon c_xi,
with c_xi finite and nonnegative. Consequently lambda_mu(theta_(t-epsilon))>=E, and these values decrease as epsilon decreases. Let their limit be ell. For each fixed xi, taking the limit in lambda_mu(theta_(t-epsilon))<=Q_t(xi)+epsilon c_xi gives ell<=Q_t(xi). Taking the infimum yields ell<=E. Thus ell=E, without interchanging an infimum and an uncontrolled limit.

The identical argument applies to theta_t+delta h. Its raw infimum lambda_delta is at least E, decreases as delta decreases, and for every fixed xi satisfies
  lambda_delta<=Q_t(xi)+delta integral_X h wedge xi^m/D_mu(xi).
The final term tends to zero. Therefore lim_(delta down to 0) lambda_delta=E for the specified arbitrary Hermitian h. The raw endpoint infimum agrees with decreasing Hermitian regularization.

Monotone convergence gives H(epsilon)->H(0)=integral_B sigma/a, with reciprocal +infinity on a=0. Hence
  lambda_mu(theta_t)=(nW/H(0))^(1/n),
  V_mu(theta_t)=nW/H(0),
where 1/(+infinity)=0. This covers a identically zero, positive-measure zero sets and arbitrarily flat zeros. No endpoint Monge–Ampère solution is assumed.

For any selection of attaining metrics xi_s, without any assumed measurability or regularity of the metric-valued selection, the scalar cost equals the same smooth nonnegative C(s) at every strict s. The scalar cost is therefore continuous and measurable. For b<t, ordinary calculus gives
  integral_0^b C(s) ds=lambda_mu(theta_0)-lambda_mu(theta_b).
These integrals increase with b and are bounded by lambda_mu(theta_0). Taking the actual endpoint limit proves
  integral_0^t C(s) ds=lambda_mu(theta_0)-lambda_mu(theta_t)<infinity.
Thus the improper integral is established for every selection, rather than assumed.

notes.summary: C: two-sided distance^k vanishing along a nonempty codimension-d zero submanifold gives all five proposed integrable cost profiles. Positive endpoint volume is equivalent to d>k; finitely many disjoint finite-order components use the smallest ratio.
notes.detailedSummary: Positive smooth density and bounded tubular Jacobians reduce inverse moments to integral rho^(d-1)/(rho^k+epsilon)^p d rho. With r=d/k, substitution gives power divergence for r<p, logarithmic divergence for r=p, and an actual finite moment limit for r>p. Applying p=1,2 to n1's scalar cost proves every proposed profile and its integrability. The endpoint inverse moment is finite exactly for r>1. For finitely many disjoint components, the smallest ratio controls the divergent terms and positivity prevents cancellation. These are geometric hypotheses, not assumed integral bounds; they do not classify arbitrary paths.
notes.text:
This note proves target C using the full volume and cost formula of n1. Fix a smooth Riemannian metric on B. The tubular hypothesis describes a nonempty zero set Z={a=0}, a smooth compact embedded real submanifold of positive codimension d, with
  c dist(b,Z)^k<=a(b)<=C dist(b,Z)^k
in a fixed sufficiently small normal tube, for c,C>0 and k>0. Outside the tube, a is bounded below by a positive constant. If the zero set is empty, a instead has a positive minimum, H(0),J(0) are finite, and the cost has a finite positive limit; no codimension/order ratio is required.

Set r=d/k. The smooth positive sigma has density bounded above and below relative to the fixed Riemannian volume. In a smaller fixed tube, normal tubular coordinates have smooth positive Jacobian bounded above and below. Radial integration in the d-dimensional normal directions contributes rho^(d-1) d rho, with positive finite factors from integration over Z and the unit normal spheres. These hypotheses justify the following comparisons without assuming any inverse-moment behavior.

For p=1,2 put M_p(epsilon)=integral_B (a+epsilon)^(-p) sigma. For a fixed tube radius R,
  M_p(epsilon) comparable to
    1+integral_0^R rho^(d-1)/(rho^k+epsilon)^p d rho
as epsilon decreases to zero. The complement contributes a bounded term. The denominators c rho^k+epsilon and C rho^k+epsilon are uniformly comparable to rho^k+epsilon, using min(c,1) and max(C,1).

Substituting q=rho^k and then q=epsilon y gives exactly
  (1/k) integral_0^(R^k) q^(r-1)/(q+epsilon)^p dq
    =(epsilon^(r-p)/k)
       integral_0^(R^k/epsilon) y^(r-1)/(1+y)^p dy.
At zero the integrand is integrable because r>0. If r<p, its tail is comparable to y^(r-p-1), an integrable power at infinity, and the scaled integral tends to a finite strictly positive constant. If r=p, the tail is comparable to 1/y, giving logarithmic growth. If r>p, the unregularized radial exponent r-p-1 is integrable at zero, and the tube and complement estimates prove M_p(0)<infinity. Monotone convergence then gives the actual finite limit. Conversely the lower tubular estimate makes M_p(0) infinite for r<=p. Therefore
  r<p: M_p(epsilon) comparable to epsilon^(r-p);
  r=p: comparable to log(1/epsilon);
  r>p: M_p(epsilon)->M_p(0), finite and positive.
The finite moments are strictly positive since a is positive away from its proper zero submanifold.

Apply p=1,2 to H=M_1 and J=M_2. By n1,
  C(t-epsilon)=K H(epsilon)^(-(n+1)/n)J(epsilon),
  K=n^(-m/n)W^(1/n)>0.
For r<1 the resulting exponent is
  -(r-1)(n+1)/n+r-2=(1-r)/n-1.
For r=1, H is logarithmic and J is comparable to epsilon^(-1). For 1<r<2, H tends to H(0)>0 and J has exponent r-2. For r=2, H has a finite positive limit and J is logarithmic. For r>2, both moments have finite positive limits. Thus every proposed profile holds:
  r<1: C(t-epsilon) comparable to epsilon^((1-r)/n-1);
  r=1: comparable to epsilon^(-1)log(1/epsilon)^(-(n+1)/n);
  1<r<2: comparable to epsilon^(r-2);
  r=2: comparable to log(1/epsilon);
  r>2: tends to K H(0)^(-(n+1)/n)J(0)>0.
Comparability means two bounds with fixed positive constants independent of sufficiently small epsilon. The hypotheses do not prescribe an exact leading coefficient in the first four regimes.

Each profile is integrable at epsilon=0. For r<1 its exponent exceeds -1. For r=1, substitution u=log(1/epsilon) gives a convergent tail integral of u^(-(n+1)/n), since (n+1)/n>1. For 1<r<2 the exponent r-2 exceeds -1. The logarithm at r=2 is integrable, and the final profile is bounded. These are quantitative geometric sufficient conditions, not assumptions of the desired improper-integral bound. Its exact total value was proved independently in n1.

By n1 the endpoint volume is positive exactly when H(0) is finite. The p=1 radial criterion makes this equivalent to r>1, or d>k. Thus positive volume can occur with a nonempty zero set; n3 establishes the bigness obstruction in that case.

For finitely many disjoint nonempty zero components Z_j, with codimensions d_j and finite orders k_j satisfying the respective two-sided bounds, choose disjoint small fixed tubes. Their complement has a positive lower bound for a. Each moment is a finite sum of tube contributions and a bounded complement contribution. Let r_*=min_j d_j/k_j. If r_*<p, a minimum-ratio component has the strongest divergent power epsilon^(r_*-p); larger-ratio contributions have lower growth or stay bounded. If r_*=p, at least one contribution is logarithmic and all others are bounded. If r_*>p, every unregularized moment is finite and monotone convergence gives the finite total limit. All contributions are positive, so cancellation cannot occur. The five profiles therefore hold with r replaced by r_*, and positive endpoint volume is equivalent to r_*>1. When r_*>2 the exact limit uses the actual total H(0),J(0).

Evidence: the exponent identity is algebraic for every admissible real r. The small program checks.py also verifies it at 18 rational (n,r) pairs; those finite checks are not the proof of the continuous statement. Run "python3 checks.py"; artifacts/check_inputs.json and artifacts/check_output.json retain its inputs and outputs. No additional PDE or uncertain indispensable premise is needed beyond n1 and the stated geometric hypotheses. This restricted result does not classify arbitrary paths.

notes.summary: D: theta_t is big exactly when a has no zero, proved against every genuine quasi-psh potential using distributional smooth tests. Normalized projective examples are nonclosed and nonbig but have V=(m+1)(m-1)/m>0, logarithmic cost for m=2 and a positive finite cost limit for m>2.
notes.detailedSummary: Pairing a purported strict current with f alpha^m for arbitrary smooth nonnegative base f removes the potential by distributional Stokes and forces a to be uniformly positive. No singular current is restricted to a fiber. Conversely a positive minimum gives a smooth strict metric. The affine Fubini–Study density and radial substitution prove mass one and the exact probability law m x^(m-1)dx for the specified global a. Its sole zero is quadratic with codimension 2m. Exact moments give the full endpoint volume and the claimed costs through n1. Rational and Decimal checks corroborate implemented arithmetic only; they do not certify the PDE or exhaust Gauduchon tests.
notes.text:
This note proves target D, using n1 for full-test values and n2 for geometric profiles. Consider any genuine global quasi-psh u with
  T=theta_t+dd^c u>=delta h,
where delta>0. Genuine quasi-psh local integrability makes u a global distribution. It need not be finite on any particular fiber. Compactness and positivity give c>0 such that h>=c Omega, where Omega=alpha+w.

For every smooth nonnegative f on B, F=f alpha^m is a smooth strongly semipositive (m,m) test form on X. It satisfies dd^c F=0: its coefficients and factors are pulled back from B, and dd^c F would have horizontal bidegree (m+1,m+1) on an m-fold. Distributional Stokes gives
  integral_X dd^c u wedge F=integral_X u dd^c F=0.
Pair positivity of T-delta c Omega with F. Using alpha^(m+1)=0 and integral_C w=1 gives
  0<=integral_X (T-delta c Omega) wedge f alpha^m
    =integral_B f(a-delta c)alpha^m.
These are smooth test pairings; no restriction or trace of T on a fiber occurs. Since this holds for every such f, continuity forces a>=delta c everywhere: a smooth nonnegative bump supported where a-delta c<0 would contradict it. Thus a zero excludes EVERY genuine strict quasi-psh representative, including a potential singular on the whole zero fiber.

Conversely, if a has no zero, its compact minimum is positive. Theta_t=alpha+aw is then smooth strictly positive and dominates a positive multiple of h. The genuine potential u=0 proves bigness. Consequently theta_t is big if and only if a has no zero. Combining this with n2 gives positive-volume nonbig endpoints whenever the zero set satisfies the tubular criterion with minimum ratio greater than one. This is a criterion for these product backgrounds, not a general positive-volume bigness theorem.

For the explicit example, on projective m-space, m>=2, use the chart Z_0!=0 with z_j=Z_j/Z_0 and rho^2=sum_j |z_j|^2. Define
  kappa=dd^c log(1+rho^2).
On other charts the potentials are log(sum |Z_j|^2/|Z_i|^2). Their differences are logarithms of squared moduli of nonvanishing holomorphic transition functions, hence have zero partial barpartial. They glue to a smooth real closed form. The matrix of the displayed potential is
  g_(j bar l)=((1+rho^2)delta_(jl)-bar z_j z_l)/(1+rho^2)^2.
Its radial eigenvalue is (1+rho^2)^(-2) and its m-1 transverse eigenvalues are (1+rho^2)^(-1). Thus kappa is positive and the determinant is (1+rho^2)^(-(m+1)). With dd^c=i partial barpartial/(2 pi),
  kappa^m=(m!/pi^m)(1+rho^2)^(-(m+1))dLeb_(2m).
Each i dz_j wedge dbar z_j contributes twice dx_j wedge dy_j, and the top wedge contributes m!, proving the coefficient.

The Euclidean sphere in 2m dimensions has area 2 pi^m/(m-1)!, obtained by comparing product and radial Gaussian integrals. Radial integration therefore gives
  2m rho^(2m-1)/(1+rho^2)^(m+1)d rho.
The omitted projective hyperplane has real codimension two and zero measure for a smooth volume. Substitute x=rho^2/(1+rho^2), so dx=2rho/(1+rho^2)^2 d rho. The density becomes exactly m x^(m-1)dx on [0,1), of total mass one. This proves integral_B kappa^m=1 with the specified normalization.

The function
  a([Z])=sum_(j=1)^m |Z_j|^2/sum_(j=0)^m |Z_j|^2
is unchanged by nonzero homogeneous scaling, hence global and smooth. It is nonnegative and has sole zero p=[1:0:...:0]. Near p, a=rho^2/(1+rho^2) is comparable to rho^2. Distance for any fixed smooth Riemannian metric is comparable to rho in a small coordinate ball. The zero therefore has d=2m, k=2, r=m and satisfies the exact tubular assumptions. On the compact complement a has a positive lower bound. The radial substitution proves that its law under sigma=kappa^m is m x^(m-1)dx on [0,1].

Take alpha=kappa and C=projective one-space. Any specified smooth positive probability area form w works; a concrete choice is normalized Fubini–Study, whose mass-one calculation is the same computation with m=1. Then W=1, sigma=kappa^m is a smooth positive probability, and mu=sigma wedge w has total mass one. For any t>0, theta_s=kappa+(a+t-s)w is strictly positive for s<t and its semipositive endpoint is nef. Because a is nonconstant,
  d theta_s=da wedge w
is nonzero somewhere: wedging a nonzero horizontal one-form with the positive vertical area form is injective. Thus both path and endpoint are genuinely nonclosed.

The exact probability law gives
  H(epsilon)=m integral_0^1 x^(m-1)/(x+epsilon)dx,
  J(epsilon)=m integral_0^1 x^(m-1)/(x+epsilon)^2 dx,
  H(0)=m/(m-1).
For m>2, J(0)=m/(m-2); for m=2 it is infinite. These give FULL-test values through n1, with actual smooth balanced minimizers at every strict point:
  V_mu(theta_(t-epsilon))=(m+1)/H(epsilon),
  V_mu(theta_t)=(m+1)(m-1)/m>0.
The zero at p and the every-potential argument prove theta_t is not big. No endpoint PDE or selected-test-only upper bound is used.

For m=2, elementary integration gives
  H(epsilon)=2[1-epsilon log((1+epsilon)/epsilon)],
  J(epsilon)=2[log((1+epsilon)/epsilon)-1/(1+epsilon)].
Hence H->2 and J/log(1/epsilon)->2. The exact cost formula implies
  C(t-epsilon)/log(1/epsilon)->3^(-2/3)2^(-1/3)>0.
For m>2, the actual limit is
  C(t-epsilon)->(m+1)^(-m/(m+1))
    [m/(m-1)]^(-(m+2)/(m+1))[m/(m-2)]>0.
These agree with the r=2 and r>2 profiles of n2. Every minimizing selection has these costs and the finite improper identity of n1.

For every integer m>=2, polynomial division also gives the exact strict-point expression
  H(epsilon)=m[sum_(j=0)^(m-2)(-epsilon)^j/(m-1-j)
    +(-epsilon)^(m-1)log((1+epsilon)/epsilon)].
Indeed I_0=log((1+epsilon)/epsilon) and I_p=1/p-epsilon I_(p-1) for I_p=integral_0^1 x^p/(x+epsilon)dx. Thus no numerical extrapolation is needed.

Evidence: run "python3 checks.py". Its deterministic 90-digit Decimal and rational calculations use m=2,3,4,5 and epsilon=1,0.1,10^(-3),10^(-6),10^(-10), as recorded in artifacts/check_inputs.json. H and J are computed using separate integral recurrences; costs are compared with central finite differences of lambda in epsilon. The program checks positivity, exact rational endpoint constants, 18 exponent samples and AM–GM on 30 diagonal matrices. All checks passed; artifacts/check_output.json records the output and environment. Maximum observed derivative relative error was below 9.38 times 10^(-42). For m=2, the observed C/log was approximately 0.365000 versus the proved limit approximately 0.381571; the displayed exact formulas explain slow logarithmic convergence.

These are finite exact algebra checks and numerical observations, not proof certificates or exhaustive Gauduchon tests. Global minimizing-test and current claims follow from the arguments and their permitted foundation, not execution success. No resource-heavy local computation was undertaken.

notes.detailedSummary: The compact Kähler product has closed nef representatives A=alpha+(a0+t)w and B0=tw. Their Morse expression is nWa0, equal to n1's endpoint volume for every smooth product probability. The permitted cohomological Morse theorem applies precisely in the compact Kähler closed-nef setting, and its primary statement and volume convention were checked. For nonconstant a, differential formulas, explicit density dependence and a smooth-gauge variation of top integrals prevent cohomological misidentification. Any permitted core decomposition would yield a genuine strict potential by Demailly–Păun and the granted global potential consequence, contradicting n3. notes.text:
This note proves E and completes the exact restricted A–E reconstruction using n1–n3. The results remain unverified drafts relative to the expressly permitted established foundations. They do not resolve the original general P14 programme or establish literature priority.

For a=a0>=0, set A=alpha+(a0+t)w and B0=tw, with n=m+1. The compact product is Kähler with Omega=alpha+w. Both representatives are smooth d-closed; A is strictly positive since t>0 and B0 is semipositive. Their real cohomology classes are nef in the ordinary compact Kähler sense, since adding any positive multiple of Omega gives strictly positive representatives.

Exterior algebra yields
  A^n=n(a0+t)alpha^m wedge w,
  A^(n-1) wedge B0=t alpha^m wedge w.
Thus
  integral_X A^n-n integral_X A^(n-1) wedge B0=nW a0.
For ANY smooth positive base probability sigma, H(epsilon)=1/(a0+epsilon). Its endpoint value is 1/a0 for a0>0 and infinite for a0=0. The proved endpoint formula of n1 therefore gives V_mu(theta_t)=nW a0 in both cases. This proves equality of the Morse expression with the endpoint fixed-density volume independently of sigma.

The exact permitted comparison was checked against Tosatti, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.30153v2, dated 8 September 2026, Theorem 1.1 on printed page 1. For nef real (1,1) cohomology classes P,Q on a compact Kähler manifold, it states
  Vol(P-Q)>=integral P^n-n integral P^(n-1)Q.
Here Vol is ordinary cohomological volume, defined to be zero outside the pseudoeffective cone. Applying it to P=[A], Q=[B0] gives
  Vol([A]-[B0])>=nW a0=V_mu(theta_t).
This is the claimed comparison in its precise closed-nef compact Kähler setting. The established theorem is imported, not newly reproved.

For nonconstant a the actual differential information is
  d theta_s=da wedge w,
  d(theta_s^m)=m da wedge alpha^(m-1) wedge w,
  dd^c(theta_s^m)=m dd^c a wedge alpha^(m-1) wedge w.
The first differential is nonzero somewhere because B is connected and a is nonconstant. Such backgrounds do not define closed (1,1) cohomology classes. Their full values are nW/H(epsilon), retaining the specified inverse moment against sigma; the closed-class Morse theorem does not apply to theta_t itself.

Ordinary top integrals can fail smooth dd^c gauge invariance in this very family. Consider the global base function a and
  F(q)=integral_X(theta_t+q dd^c a)^n
    =n integral_B a(alpha+q dd^c a)^m.
For sufficiently small real q, alpha+q dd^c a stays positive by compactness. Differentiating this finite polynomial and integrating by parts against the closed alpha^(m-1) gives
  F'(0)=nm integral_B a dd^c a wedge alpha^(m-1)
    =-nm integral_B(i/(2 pi))partial a wedge barpartial a wedge alpha^(m-1)<0
for nonconstant a. The last integrand is nonnegative and positive where da is nonzero, an open nonempty region. This proves actual failure of top-integral gauge invariance with the required normalization. The Gauduchon quotient is nevertheless smoothly dd^c-gauge invariant by the different Stokes pairing proved in n1.

Density dependence is explicit as well. At a strict point set f=L^(-1)-H and sigma_q=(1+q f)sigma for sufficiently small real q. This is a smooth positive probability, since f is bounded and integral f sigma=0. Its inverse moment is
  H_q=H+q(J-H^2).
For nonconstant a, J-H^2 is the strictly positive variance of L^(-1) under the positive probability sigma. Thus nW/H_q changes with the specified product density. It is not a cohomological quantity.

Now suppose a has a zero and that, for some smooth global real f, there is a decomposition
  theta_t+dd^c f=chi+beta,
where chi is smooth real d-closed, [chi] is nef, integral_X chi^n>0, and beta is smooth semipositive. The permitted primary statement of Demailly–Păun, https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0105176v2, Theorem 2.12 on printed pages 12–13, was checked: on a compact Kähler manifold a nef real (1,1) class with positive top self-intersection contains a closed Kähler current. It gives T_chi in [chi] with T_chi>=delta Omega for some delta>0.

The separately permitted compact Kähler ddbar lemma and global quasi-psh-potential consequence provide
  T_chi=chi+dd^c v
